speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are at a critical juncture in the development of our energy market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since the 1990s, we have operated an open energy market and this has served us well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A competitive market has incentivised generation companies (gencos) to bring in new and more efficient technologies and they also offered more choices for consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many consumers have also enjoyed lower electricity prices as a result.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, the energy landscape has changed drastically, and new sources of supply risks and volatilities have emerged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, heightened volatility arising from tight power generation capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This has emerged in liberalised markets all around the world, where capacity planting decisions are made by private gencos based on short-term price signals in the wholesale electricity market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For these gencos, high electricity prices typically signal that capacity is tight and that new generation plantings are, therefore, needed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, very often, these price signals can come a bit too late and it takes about four to five years typically to build a new generator.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The time lag between the price signals and the construction of new generators, therefore, leads to shortages of generation capacity and can lead to sharp spikes and protracted elevation of electricity prices and even blackouts during periods of system stress, as we saw in some cities last year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, supply risks and volatility arising from disruptions in global gas supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As we rely on imported natural gas for almost all of our electricity production, global supply and demand shocks will spill over into our domestic electricity market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As fuel prices surged last year, our electricity market was severely tested.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Gencos were reluctant to contract for gas, for fear that they would be left holding on to expensive gas inventories should prices moderate subsequently.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This, in turn, increased the risks of gas shortfalls and it caused prices in the wholesale electricity market to surge.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We observed this in the fourth quarter of last year, where six electricity retailers exited the market as they were not sufficiently prepared to deal with the extreme market volatilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While affected consumers did not experience any disruptions to their power supply, some of them experienced inconveniences as well as price surges while sourcing for alternative electricity retail contracts and they faced higher prices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These sources of volatility have tested our energy market over the past year, with the ongoing energy crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since the fourth quarter of last year, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) has put in place emergency measures which have helped to stabilise the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, Members of the House, this is unlikely to be the last energy crunch that we will face, and we would need to be even more prepared for a more volatile global energy market going forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will, therefore, need to introduce safeguards to manage the risks of volatilities in our energy market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last month, the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) announced that it would be introducing guardrails to strengthen our energy market in three key areas – power generation, gas supply and electricity retail markets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These guardrails are intended to ensure that our energy market continues to function well even under volatile conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The tender will be conducted in advance of when the new capacity is needed, taking into account the lead time which is required for construction and development.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Should there be inadequate private sector interest to plant new capacity, EMA will step in to build the required new capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are the regulations requiring gencos to maintain sufficient fuel for power generation and the standby fuel facility to guard against risks of gas supply disruptions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will also be working with the industry to explore ways to aggregate gas procurement and obtain longer-term, more secure contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The regulatory enhancements include raising the qualifying criteria so that only credible industry participants with sufficient financial strength and sustainable business propositions will be allowed to retail electricity to consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As for whether EMA will prohibit retailers from prematurely terminating contracts with their consumers, this is already the case under the Code of Conduct for Retail Electricity Licensees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Retailers cannot unilaterally terminate contracts unless under stipulated conditions, such as if they are exiting the sector, or consumers are insolvent or had a breach of contract.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will be launching a consultation in the coming weeks on specific proposals to enhance the regulatory requirements for retailers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For consumers, EMA will look into tightening the eligibility criteria for Wholesale Electricity Price (WEP) plans, so that only larger consumers who are better equipped to deal with the risks of price volatilities would be allowed to enter into such plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA is also in discussion with market participants on operational measures to strengthen the wholesale electricity market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, our experience over the past year has demonstrated that a robust wholesale electricity market can have a stabilising influence on the broader retail market, and is an important pillar of our efforts to strengthen the electricity retail market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is fundamental and foundational to our ability to grow our economy, to create good jobs for our people and to maintain our quality of life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will continue to do its best to ensure that Singaporeans can continue to enjoy a stable, secure and reliable source of electricity for years to come.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have just two supplementary questions for the Second Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I read recently that Indonesia will extend its gas supply contract to Singapore by about five years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I think it was announced over the past week.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, reportedly, based on a Reuters article, distribution volume is reportedly 30% to 40% lower but at higher prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in light of these guardrails which, I recognise, strengthen our gas supply agreements, what is the expected change in the mix between piped natural gas and liquified natural gas (LNG) over the next five years and beyond when this new contract expires?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Currently, the majority of the gas supply comes from piped natural gas and the balance from liquefied natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the Member would have known, we have our Singapore LNG (SLNG) terminal and this terminal allows us to import liquefied natural gas from all over the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But the drop will be made up for by imports through LNG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the shortened period today, the new gas contract of five years, is also a function of the volatility in terms of the pricing that countries all over the world are going through and experiencing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the price is pegged at too high a level, then obviously, the ability for us to import LNG from other parts of the world would become more attractive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is a commercial arrangement between GSPL and the Indonesian entity, just like for the imports of natural gas from other entities, those are also private commercial agreements.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think the Government should comment on these things.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the point about how these gas prices will translate into higher cost, natural gas, over the medium term, is still one of the most environmentally-friendly transition fuel as we move towards our zero-carbon emission target by 2050.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As we progressively move towards renewable energy imports from the region to the ASEAN regional grid, as we adopt and intensify our land use for solar power adoption, as we move towards funding, going into more research into the carbon capture storage solutions, as we go into hydrogen – there is a Parliamentary Question, if we get there, which I will speak more on later – we believe that the dependency in the long haul on natural gas will start to drop.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, I think the caution that I want to add to this House is that the transition towards renewable energy may not necessarily result in cheaper electricity, because there is a cost in terms of adopting green sources of renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have just one follow-up supplementary question for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will EMA or MTI consider strengthening retail consumer protection and safeguards such as the ease of transfer ability or novation of consumer contracts to alternative retailers, or also maybe a recourse mechanism for a more cost-efficient and expeditious consumer-related dispute resolution.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the short answer is, we will be consulting more, and we will be tweaking and also improving on the existing suite.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the key takeaway is that, the energy market, the Open Electricity Market (OEM) has worked well for us thus far; it has resulted in a lot more efficiencies in terms of the pricing mechanism.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What has worked, has worked based on a certain band of volatility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In this particular period of time and in the foreseeable three to five years, as I have shared in my earlier speech, the volatility range has increased significantly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the existing frameworks would now have to be tweaked, to take into consideration the heightened range, the increase range of volatilities and it is timely for us to also do this public consultation exercise to see how we can work collectively together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have also exhorted the House: Members, if you have ideas, please share them with us, we are happy to take them on board.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also good to hear that some of these protections for retail consumers will be progressively rolled out from 2023.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I just have one supplementary question and it is whether or not there will be consideration given to better consumer education about the choices that they are facing, in terms of which retailer to go for.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think some of the feedback that we often get is that the various options available, the various contractual options, the lock-in periods, even the rates that we are paying, the differing rates; some consumers can find that quite confusing and I am just wondering whether there will be better consumer education or sharper consumer education, so that the consumers do not think, "Hey, there are more protections coming in, therefore, there is no risk or lower risk".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because, as the Minister shared earlier, there is still volatility that we expect in the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, whether or not we can start looking at sharpening the consumer education, about the consequences of the choices that they might make.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will certainly improve, we will certainly consider – we would not just consider, we will certainly add on in terms of strengthening consumer education.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But for the Member's information and perhaps to add to her understanding: under the Electricity Act currently, EMA has issued and published on its website, the Code of Conduct for retail electricity licensees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Code of Conduct sets out the minimum standards of performance which retail electricity licensees have to adhere to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The second point, the code of conduct also prohibits retailers from unilaterally terminating contracts with consumers, unless under stipulated conditions – such as if they are exiting the sector, or consumers are insolvent, or had breached the terms of their contract with the retailer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the third point is that there are safeguards in retailer exits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Exiting retailers must also approach other retailers to seek their interest and agreement to accept the novation of the contracts on the same terms and conditions before the consumer can be transferred to SP group under the default supply arrangement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, there are safeguards today but we will continue to strengthen the education to all consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I want to also seek Members of the House, including Ms He, to underscore the fact that, at the end of the day, energy conservation must still remain the foundation of how we are going to move forward in our overall energy transition story.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The question really was – the point I was trying to get at is that, yes, I know that they are required to have certain requirements when they signed a contract with the consumer; there is a checklist, I believe.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am just wondering whether the consumers truly understand, or whether it just becomes one of those check boxes that get ticked.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And so, whether has EMA, for example, surveyed how helpful this checklist is, whether the buyers truly understand what they are signing as opposed to, that they kind of "half understand" but just signed a sign a piece of paper.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And, whether this is also provided in all four languages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will be part of the public consult that we are going out with to see how we nuance it and reach a wider group of Singapore population, and at the same time, improve the communications to them.
